title: Cristaux (1970). Gribouillis et calculs divers : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Grothendieck is working in his Tannakian picture of motives (c. 1967-70). M is a motive over a p-adic field. T_p(M) is its p-adic (étale) realization, a Q_p-space with an action of the Galois group π = Gal(K̄/K). T_Hdg(M) is a bigraded realization (Hodge, or more likely the Hodge-graded de Rham realization) with pieces T_Hdg^{i,j}. C should be read as C_p, the completed algebraic closure, and C(1) as the Tate twist with its Galois action.

Line 1 is the Hodge-Tate decomposition, as a π-equivariant isomorphism:
T_p(M) ⊗_{Q_p} C ≅ ⊕ T_Hdg(M)^{i,j} ⊗ C(-i).

Step 1. Choose a C-linear (not Galois-equivariant) trivialization ρ: C(1) ≅ C. This turns the decomposition into a bigraded C-linear isomorphism ρ̃: T_p ⊗ C ≅ T_Hdg ⊗ C.

Step 2. Doing this for all M gives a point ρ̃ ∈ P(C). Here P is the torsor of tensor isomorphisms between the p-adic and Hodge fibre functors, a torsor under the motivic Galois group G.

Step 3. If ρ' = uρ with u ∈ C*, then ρ̃' differs from ρ̃ by i_1(u^{-1}). Here i_1: G_m → G is the weight/Hodge cocharacter that acts on the (i,j) piece through the first index.

Step 4. So ρ ↦ ρ̃ is a map C(1)* → P(C), equivariant for C* (acting on P through i_1^{-1}) and for π. Geometrically it is a morphism of G_m-schemes V(C(-1))* → P_C, where V(C(-1))* = V(Z_p(-1))*_C is the G_m-torsor of trivializations of the Tate twist.

Step 5. This morphism must be compatible with two pairs of cocharacters: (j_1, j_2) on the p-adic/Galois side and (i_1, i_2) on the Hodge side. Grothendieck says (j_1, j_2) is obtained from (i_1, i_2) by descent, once one chooses the isomorphism G_L ⊗_L C ≅ G_C attached to a ρ̃. In modern terms, the Hodge-Tate cocharacter of the p-adic realization is a twisted form of (conjugate to) the Hodge cocharacter.

The point of the page is to encode p-adic Hodge-Tate comparison as a G_m-equivariant section of the period torsor. The coordinate ring of V(C(-1))* is ⊕_n C(n) = C[t, t^{-1}], which is exactly Fontaine's B_HT. So the boxed map is precisely a B_HT-valued point of the comparison torsor.
errors: C must be C_p (or the completion of an algebraic closure), not the complex numbers. The decomposition is π-equivariant only with Galois-twisted coefficients C(-i), and holds only for Hodge-Tate realizations (proved by Tate for p-divisible groups; in general much later by Faltings and others). At this date it is a conjectural input.
The map C(1)* → P(C) is only equivariant once the semilinear π-action is taken into account. The page states this loosely ('espaces à opérateurs de π').
Sign and normalization conventions are left implicit: whether i_1(u^{-1}) or i_1(u), and the twist C(-i) versus C(-j). These are harmless.
The descent statement for (j_1, j_2) from (i_1, i_2) is asserted, not proved. It amounts to a Hodge-Tate/Hodge cocharacter comparison that is still conjectural for general motives.

ideas.what: Hodge-Tate decomposition of the p-adic realization of a motive, matched with its Hodge bigrading
ideas.usually_credited_to: Tate (1967, p-divisible groups); conjectured in general by Tate and Grothendieck; proved by Faltings (1988) and others
ideas.where_published: Possibly alluded to in his 1970 ICM talk 'Groupes de Barsotti-Tate et cristaux' (mysterious functor), but not in this form

ideas.what: Viewing the comparison as a point of the torsor P of tensor isomorphisms between realization fibre functors, under the motivic Galois group
ideas.modern_name: Period torsor Isom^⊗(ω_et, ω_Hdg) in the Tannakian formalism

ideas.what: The G_m-equivariant morphism V(C(-1))* → P_C, i.e. the comparison as a section of the period torsor over the G_m-torsor of trivializations of C_p(1), whose coordinate ring is B_HT = ⊕ C_p(n)
ideas.modern_name: Fontaine's B_HT-valued point of the comparison torsor / Hodge-Tate cocharacter (Serre, Sen)

ideas.what: The Hodge-Tate cocharacter (j_1, j_2) arises by descent/twisting from the Hodge cocharacter (i_1, i_2) via an isomorphism of motivic Galois groups G_L ⊗ C ≅ G_C
ideas.modern_name: Hodge-Tate cocharacter conjugate to the Hodge (Mumford-Tate) cocharacter; p-adic analogue of Mumford-Tate compatibility
ideas.usually_credited_to: Serre (1979), Pink, Wintenberger; motivic version folklore

missed.claim: Around 1970 Grothendieck formulated the Hodge-Tate comparison Tannakianly: a choice of trivialization of C_p(1) gives a point of the étale/Hodge comparison torsor, and varying it gives a G_m-equivariant map from Spec of ⊕ C_p(n) into P. This is in substance Fontaine's later B_HT period-ring formalism and Serre's Hodge-Tate cocharacter, expressed motivically, about a decade earlier.
missed.quote: un hom de G_{m C}-schémas V(C(-1))^* → P_C ... V(Z_p(-1))^*_C
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It documents that the 'period ring = coordinate ring of a torsor' viewpoint, and the comparison between Hodge-Tate and Hodge cocharacters as descent along motivic Galois groups, were in Grothendieck's motivic programme. This is relevant to the history of p-adic Hodge theory and the 'mysterious functor'.

missed.claim: The compatibility of (j_1, j_2) with (i_1, i_2) by descent is a motivic Hodge-Tate/Hodge cocharacter comparison. It is left unproved and is still open for general motives.
missed.quote: (j_1,j_2) résulte par descente de i_1,i_2, quand on choisit l'isom. G_L⊗_L C ≃ G_C associé à un ρ̃
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a precursor to the Mumford-Tate-type statements for Hodge-Tate cocharacters, which are known only in special cases (abelian varieties).

deep.surprise_reason: This is a concise, early Tannakian treatment of the Hodge-Tate comparison as a G_m-equivariant point of the motivic period torsor. In substance it anticipates Fontaine's B_HT and Serre's Hodge-Tate cocharacter, and it is not in Grothendieck's published texts. However, it is a sketch, and the general idea of period torsors is known to come from Grothendieck.
transcription_corrections: The page is written on the back of a typed page from the cycle-class exposé (numbered pages 33/34 with 3.8-3.10); the handwriting is independent of it.
'Hom_{Spec ?}' – the subscript under Hom is a hastily written 'Spec' plus something (likely 'Spec L' or a base); unclear.
The inserted words below 'un hom de' are hard to read; 'étendant[?]' is doubtful, possibly 'définissant' or 'élément'.
'T_{Hdg C}' should be read as T_Hdg(M) ⊗ C.
The boxed arrow C(1)^* → P(C) has an arrow drawn from it down to V(C(-1))^* → P_C, indicating that they are the same map.
